questions.q: How is Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmitted?
ch: By inhaled airborne droplet nuclei that reach the alveoli
By the faecal-oral route from contaminated water
By transfusion of contaminated blood products
By an arthropod vector during a blood meal
By direct contact with broken skin
questions.exp: TB spreads by inhaled airborne droplet nuclei of 1 to 5 microns that travel to the alveoli. This is why airborne isolation is required.
why: TB is not a faecal-oral pathogen.
Bloodborne transmission is not the route of spread.
There is no insect vector for TB.
Skin contact does not transmit pulmonary TB.

questions.q: What distinguishes latent tuberculosis infection from active disease?
ch: Latent infection is symptomatic but non-infectious
Latent infection is asymptomatic, non-infectious and contained by cell-mediated immunity
Latent infection always shows cavitation on chest X-ray
Latent infection cannot be detected by any test
questions.exp: Latent infection is contained by cell-mediated immunity: asymptomatic and non-infectious, with a 5 to 10 percent lifetime risk of reactivation that rises with HIV, TNF inhibitors and diabetes.
why: Latent infection is asymptomatic by definition.
Cavitation indicates active reactivation disease.
Latent infection is treated with single-drug or short-course regimens, not RIPE.
TST and IGRA detect infection, though they cannot separate latent from active.

questions.q: What is the hallmark histological finding in tuberculosis?
ch: Caseating granuloma with Langhans giant cells
questions.exp: The classic histology is a caseating granuloma with Langhans giant cells, driven by the Th1 and CD4 response with TNF-alpha and macrophage activation.
why: Eosinophilic infiltration suggests parasitic or allergic disease.
Non-caseating granulomas are characteristic of sarcoidosis.
Neutrophilic abscess describes pyogenic infection.
Hyaline membranes are the pathology of ARDS.

questions.q: Which test is the gold standard for confirming active pulmonary tuberculosis?
ch: Serum antibody testing for mycobacterial antigens
Tuberculin skin test read at 48 to 72 hours
Interferon-gamma release assay on whole blood
Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and culture
questions.exp: Sputum AFB smear and culture is the confirmatory gold standard, with NAAT or Xpert MTB/RIF for rapid detection and rifampin resistance. Three sputum specimens should be obtained.
why: Serology is not a reliable diagnostic test for TB.
The tuberculin skin test detects infection, not active disease.
IGRA also detects infection only and cannot distinguish latent from active.
Imaging supports the diagnosis but does not confirm the organism.

questions.q: Why does reactivation tuberculosis localise to the upper lobes?
ch: Because the upper lobes have thinner pleura
Because bronchi are wider in the upper lobes
Because high oxygen tension there favours the aerobic organism
questions.exp: M. tuberculosis is aerobic, and the higher oxygen tension in the apices favours its growth. That is why reactivation causes upper-lobe cavitation.
why: Lymphatic drainage does not explain the apical predilection.
Pleural thickness is irrelevant to organism growth.
Bronchial calibre does not determine the site of reactivation.
Gravity-dependent drainage would favour lower lobes.

questions.q: Which adverse effect is characteristic of ethambutol?
questions.exp: Ethambutol causes optic neuritis. Check baseline visual acuity and red-green colour discrimination, and teach the patient to report any change in vision.
why: Raised uric acid is caused by pyrazinamide.
Myelosuppression is a feature of linezolid in MDR regimens.
Peripheral neuropathy is caused by isoniazid and prevented with pyridoxine.
Orange-red secretions are caused by rifampin.

questions.q: Why must pyridoxine be co-administered with isoniazid?
questions.exp: Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy, and pyridoxine prevents it. It is essential in pregnancy, alcoholism, diabetes, malnutrition and HIV.
why: Isoniazid is hepatotoxic, but pyridoxine does not prevent that; LFT monitoring does.
Optic neuritis is an ethambutol effect.
Hyperuricaemia is a pyrazinamide effect.
Pyridoxine is protective, not potentiating.

questions.q: A patient is about to start infliximab. Why must latent tuberculosis be excluded first?
ch: Because infliximab is directly toxic to mycobacteria
Because TNF-alpha maintains granuloma integrity, and blocking it allows reactivation
Because infliximab causes false-positive sputum cultures
Because infliximab is contraindicated with rifampin
questions.exp: TNF-alpha maintains granuloma integrity. Anti-TNF biologics such as infliximab allow latent TB to reactivate, so screening is mandatory before starting.
why: Optic neuritis is an ethambutol effect.
Infliximab has no antimycobacterial activity.
It does not interfere with culture results.
Drug interaction is not the reason for pre-treatment screening.

questions.q: What is the standard treatment regimen for drug-susceptible active pulmonary tuberculosis?
ch: Bedaquiline, linezolid and pretomanid for 6 months
RIPE for 2 months then isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months
Rifampin and isoniazid for 2 months total
questions.exp: Standard therapy is RIPE (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for a 2-month intensive phase, then isoniazid and rifampin for a 4-month continuation phase, six months total, adjusted for susceptibilities.
why: A single dose does not treat active tuberculosis.
BPaL is the regimen for MDR or XDR disease, not drug-susceptible TB.
Isoniazid monotherapy treats latent infection, not active disease, and would breed resistance.
Two months of two drugs is inadequate for active disease.

questions.q: A patient who received BCG vaccination has a positive tuberculin skin test. How can this pitfall be resolved?
ch: Assume the result is a true positive and start RIPE
Assume the result is false and take no further action
Perform a sputum smear as the screening test
Repeat the skin test in the other arm
Use an interferon-gamma release assay, which is unaffected by BCG
questions.exp: BCG can cause a false-positive tuberculin skin test. An IGRA avoids this pitfall because it is not confounded by prior BCG vaccination.
why: Starting four-drug therapy on an unconfirmed positive is inappropriate; active disease must first be established.
Dismissing the result risks missing genuine infection.
Sputum testing is for active disease, not for screening asymptomatic infection.
Repeating the same test in the other arm reproduces the same confounding.

questions.q: Which broad division of lung cancer accounts for roughly 85% of cases?
questions.exp: Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for about 85% of cases and includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell and large cell. Small cell lung cancer, a neuroendocrine tumour, makes up about 15%.
why: Carcinoid tumours are a small minority.
Mesothelioma arises from pleura, not lung parenchyma.
Metastases to the lung are common but are not primary lung cancer.
Small cell accounts for about 15%.

questions.q: Which subtype is the most common and the most frequent type in non-smokers?
questions.exp: Adenocarcinoma is now the most common subtype and the most frequent type in non-smokers. It is peripheral and carries targetable driver mutations such as EGFR, ALK, ROS1 and KRAS G12C.
why: Small cell is central, aggressive and strongly smoking-associated.
Large cell is a less common NSCLC subtype.
Carcinoid is uncommon and neuroendocrine.
Squamous cell is classically central and strongly smoking-associated.

questions.q: Which is the leading cause of lung cancer in people who have never smoked?
questions.exp: Radon is the leading cause of lung cancer in non-smokers and the second leading cause overall.
why: Second-hand smoke raises risk but radon leads among non-smokers.
Asbestos is an important occupational risk but not the leading non-smoker cause.
Air pollution contributes but ranks below radon.
Prior radiation is an uncommon cause.

questions.q: Which tumour locations and smoking associations are correct?
ch: All subtypes arise centrally near the hilum
Tumour location does not correlate with subtype
Adenocarcinoma central and smoking-related; squamous peripheral
Squamous and small cell central and smoking-related; adenocarcinoma peripheral
All subtypes arise peripherally in the lung fields
questions.exp: Squamous cell and small cell are classically central and smoking-associated. Adenocarcinoma is peripheral and the most common subtype in non-smokers.
why: Adenocarcinoma is characteristically peripheral.
Location is a genuinely useful pointer to subtype.
This reverses the correct associations.
Central location is characteristic of squamous and small cell.

questions.q: What is required to establish a definitive diagnosis of lung cancer?
ch: A rising serum tumour marker on serial testing
The appearance of the mass on contrast chest CT
Avidity of the lesion on PET-CT imaging
Tissue biopsy for histology and molecular testing
questions.exp: Definitive diagnosis requires tissue: bronchoscopy, EBUS-guided nodal sampling, CT-guided core biopsy or thoracentesis cytology, providing histology and material for molecular testing.
why: Sputum cytology alone is insufficient and often non-diagnostic.
Tumour markers are not used to diagnose lung cancer.
CT characterises a mass but cannot establish histology.
PET avidity supports malignancy and aids staging but is not diagnostic.

questions.q: A patient with small cell lung cancer develops hyponatremia. Which paraneoplastic syndrome is most likely?
ch: Cushing syndrome from cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma
questions.exp: Small cell lung cancer secretes ADH, causing SIADH, and may also secrete ACTH producing Cushing syndrome. PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia is the squamous cell association.
why: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy causes digital clubbing and periostitis, not hyponatremia.
Carcinoid syndrome causes flushing and diarrhoea.
SCLC-related Cushing arises from ectopic ACTH, not an adrenal adenoma.
PTHrP hypercalcaemia is associated with squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.q: Which paraneoplastic syndrome is associated with squamous cell lung cancer?
questions.exp: Squamous cell carcinoma secretes PTHrP, causing hypercalcaemia. SIADH and ectopic ACTH belong to small cell.
why: Ectopic ACTH is a small cell association.
Lambert-Eaton is associated with small cell lung cancer.
Polycythaemia is more typical of renal cell carcinoma.
SIADH is a small cell association.

questions.q: Which criteria define eligibility for annual low-dose CT lung cancer screening?
ch: Ages 30-50 with any history of cigarette smoking
Any adult over 40 who has ever smoked cigarettes
Ages 50-80 with a 20 pack-year history, currently smoking or quit within 15 years
Only patients with a first-degree family history of lung cancer
Any patient presenting with a chronic cough
questions.exp: USPSTF recommends annual low-dose CT for ages 50 to 80 with a 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years.
why: The age band begins at 50, not 30.
Screening is not offered to all ever-smokers over 40.
Family history alone is not the screening criterion.
A chronic cough warrants diagnostic evaluation, not a screening programme.

questions.q: A patient presents with facial and neck swelling, distended neck veins and dyspnea. What complication should be suspected?
questions.exp: Superior vena cava syndrome, from central tumour compression, causes facial and neck swelling with distended neck veins and dyspnea. It is an oncologic emergency.
why: Cord compression causes back pain, weakness and incontinence.
Brain metastasis causes focal neurological deficits or seizures.
A Pancoast tumour is apical and causes Horner syndrome and arm pain.
A malignant effusion causes dyspnea and dullness, not facial swelling with distended neck veins.

questions.q: Why should molecular and PD-L1 testing be ordered on advanced non-squamous NSCLC before selecting systemic therapy?
ch: To determine whether the tumour is surgically resectable
To calculate the appropriate radiation dose
To establish the TNM stage of the disease
To confirm the histological subtype of the tumour
Because the driver mutation determines which targeted or immune therapy to use
questions.exp: Match the driver to the drug. EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS G12C, MET, RET and NTRK, plus PD-L1 expression, determine which targeted agent or checkpoint inhibitor to use, so testing should be reflexive in advanced non-squamous NSCLC.
why: Resectability is determined by stage and pulmonary reserve.
Radiation dosing is not set by molecular results.
Staging is determined by imaging and nodal sampling.
Subtype is established by histology, not molecular testing.
